interactions.label: A student classifies misoprostol as an 'acid-suppressing agent' for peptic ulcer

params.question: A student classifies misoprostol as an 'acid-suppressing agent' for peptic ulcer disease. What is the fundamental error in this classification?

answers.text: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E₁ analogue that primarily restores mucosal defence, not suppresses acid secretion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Misoprostol replaces the prostaglandins depleted by NSAIDs, reinforcing the mucosal-protection pillar. Classifying it under acid suppression conflates the two distinct pharmacological pillars of acid peptic disease management.

answers.text: Misoprostol is actually an antacid that neutralises gastric acid rather than suppressing its secretion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Antacids neutralise luminal acid by chemical buffering (e.g. aluminium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide). Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E₁ analogue that strengthens mucosal defence — a different pillar entirely.

answers.text: Misoprostol is a prokinetic agent used for gastroparesis, not peptic ulcer disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Misoprostol is not a prokinetic. It is a PGE₁ analogue used primarily for NSAID-induced ulcer prophylaxis, acting on the mucosal-protection side of the pharmacological classification.

answers.text: Misoprostol is a bismuth compound used only in Helicobacter pylori eradication regimens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Bismuth subsalicylate is the compound used in quadruple-therapy H. pylori eradication. Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin analogue — a mucosal protectant with a distinct mechanism and indication.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the two-pillar classification: acid-suppressing agents (PPIs, H₂RAs, antacids) reduce luminal acid, while mucosal-protecting agents (sucralfate, bismuth, misoprostol) reinforce the defensive barrier. Misoprostol is a PGE₁ analogue that belongs to the mucosal-protection pillar.
Well done. Recognising which pharmacological pillar a drug belongs to — acid suppression versus mucosal protection — is the first step to avoiding prescribing errors in acid peptic disease.

params.question: Metoclopramide is prescribed both as a prokinetic and as an antiemetic. Which receptor mechanisms explain this dual clinical role?

answers.text: 5-HT₃ antagonism in the gut wall and muscarinic agonism at the chemoreceptor trigger zone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. 5-HT₃ antagonists (e.g. ondansetron) are a separate antiemetic class that blocks serotonin-mediated vagal signalling. Muscarinic receptors are not the primary target for metoclopramide's antiemetic action.

answers.text: D₂ agonism in the myenteric plexus and 5-HT₄ antagonism at the chemoreceptor trigger zone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect — the receptors are reversed. Metoclopramide is a D₂ antagonist (not agonist) at the CTZ and a 5-HT₄ agonist (not antagonist) in the gut. Confusing agonism with antagonism at each site is a common exam error.

answers.text: 5-HT₄ agonism on the myenteric plexus and D₂ antagonism at the chemoreceptor trigger zone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! 5-HT₄ agonism on the myenteric plexus enhances acetylcholine release, promoting coordinated gut motility (prokinetic effect). Simultaneously, D₂ antagonism at the CTZ blocks dopamine-mediated emetic signalling (antiemetic effect).

answers.text: H₁ antagonism in the vestibular apparatus and 5-HT₄ agonism in the gut wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. H₁ antagonism is the mechanism of antihistaminic antiemetics such as promethazine and dimenhydrinate, which act on the vestibular pathway. Metoclopramide's antiemetic action is through D₂ antagonism at the CTZ, not H₁ blockade.

overallFeedback.feedback: Metoclopramide's dual role depends on two distinct receptor actions at two distinct sites: 5-HT₄ agonism on the myenteric plexus drives prokinesis, while D₂ antagonism at the chemoreceptor trigger zone provides the antiemetic effect.
Excellent. Mapping each drug to both its receptor target and its anatomical site of action is the key step that converts rote memorisation into clinical reasoning for prokinetics and antiemetics.

interactions.label: Stimulant laxatives are the preferred first-line agents for long-term management

params.question: Stimulant laxatives are the preferred first-line agents for long-term management of chronic constipation because they produce the fastest bowel response.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The statement is false. Speed of onset does not determine first-line status for chronic use. Long-term stimulant laxative use can damage the enteric nervous system (enteric neuropathy) and cause dependence, creating a cycle of worsening constipation. Safer long-term alternatives include bulk-forming and osmotic laxatives selected by mechanism.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. While stimulant laxatives are the fastest-acting class, chronic use risks drug dependence and enteric neuropathy. Mechanism-based selection — such as bulk-forming or osmotic agents — is safer for long-term management and should be matched to the patient's underlying pathophysiology.

params.question: Returning to the opening case: the 35-year-old patient's duodenal ulcer did not heal despite a 2-week course of omeprazole alone. Based on the therapeutic goal hierarchy for peptic ulcer disease, what is the most critical step that was missed?

answers.text: Prescribing a mucosal protectant such as sucralfate alongside omeprazole

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While mucosal protectants are useful adjuncts, sucralfate combined with a PPI is itself a prescribing error (sucralfate needs acidic pH). More importantly, the critical omission was failing to eradicate H. pylori — the root cause of relapse.

answers.text: Extending the omeprazole course from 2 weeks to 8 weeks without additional agents

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Extending acid suppression alone without addressing the underlying H. pylori infection would not prevent relapse. The therapeutic hierarchy places H. pylori eradication above prolonged acid suppression as the definitive step for cure.

answers.text: Eradicating Helicobacter pylori with appropriate combination antimicrobial therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! H. pylori eradication is the single most important intervention for preventing peptic ulcer relapse. Without combination therapy targeting the bacterium, acid suppression alone provides temporary symptom relief but leaves the root cause — chronic H. pylori infection — intact.

answers.text: Discontinuing ibuprofen before initiating any acid-suppressive therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Removing causative agents such as NSAIDs is indeed part of the therapeutic goal hierarchy, but in this H. pylori-positive patient, the most critical missed step is eradication of the bacterium. Both steps are needed, but eradication takes priority for relapse prevention.

overallFeedback.feedback: The five sequential goals for peptic ulcer disease are: (1) relieve symptoms, (2) heal the lesion, (3) eradicate H. pylori if positive, (4) remove causative agents, and (5) prevent complications. This patient's previous doctor addressed only symptom relief with omeprazole monotherapy, missing the most critical step — H. pylori eradication with combination antimicrobial therapy.

Well done. The therapeutic goal hierarchy ensures that treatment addresses not just symptoms but the root cause — and for H. pylori-positive peptic ulcer disease, eradication with combination therapy is the single most important step to achieve cure and prevent relapse.
